Kind
kynd
n.
Old English gecynd, nature, race, offspring, from the same root as kin. Webster 1828: race; genus; species; generic class. The noun kind and the adjective kind (benevolent) are the same word by descent — to be kind is to act according to one’s kin — but in Genesis 1 the Authorized Version uses the noun, and it is a boundary word.

Biblical Definition

Kind is the creation account’s word for a fixed boundary, and it is repeated with such insistence that the repetition is itself the doctrine. Ten times in Genesis 1 the phrase falls: the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself (Genesis 1:11); God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind (Genesis 1:21); Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind (Genesis 1:24). The Hebrew mīn marks a created category that reproduces within itself. Scripture does not tell us the taxonomic width of a kind, and the dictionary does not pretend it does; the text’s claim is narrower and firmer than a modern classification scheme. It says God made distinct categories, each bearing seed in itself, and that the categories are His and not an artifact of description. Paul assumes the same structure when arguing for the resurrection: All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds (1 Corinthians 15:39). The doctrine of creation and the doctrine of the resurrection body rest on the same premise — God assigns kinds, and He keeps them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines KIND as a noun: race; genus; generic class; sort, in a sense more loose than genus. Webster derives it from the same root as kin, and notes the adjective sense — disposed to do good — grows from the idea of acting according to one’s nature or kindred.

expand to see more

KIND, n. [Sax. cynd, kind, nature, kindred.] — Race; genus; generic class; as in Scripture, the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind. Sort, in a sense more loose than genus; as, a kind of stuff or silk. Nature; natural propensity or determination.

Webster cites Genesis directly under the noun, which tells us how the word was heard in 1828: kind was a category in nature, not a category in the mind of the classifier. That is the whole disagreement with the modern account, and it was already implicit in the dictionary two decades before the Origin of Species.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:11 — "And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so."

Genesis 1:21 — "And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good."

Genesis 1:24 — "And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so."

1 Corinthians 15:39 — "All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds."

Modern Corruption

Kind is corrupted from a created boundary into a convenient human label — a name we assign to a slice of a continuum — which removes from Genesis 1 the one thing it repeats ten times, and which is then extended from biology to the body itself.

expand to see more

The Darwinian account does not merely propose a mechanism; it denies the category. If every living thing stands on an unbroken continuum, then kind is a word we impose on a gradient for convenience, and Genesis 1’s tenfold refrain describes nothing real. The dictionary’s position is that God created distinct kinds, each reproducing after itself, and that the boundaries are His. This is not a claim that the biblical kind maps onto the modern species — it plainly does not, and honest advocates on every side grant the mismatch. It is a claim that the categories are given rather than constructed. Everything in Genesis 1 that is repeated is repeated on purpose, and this phrase is repeated more than any other.

The deeper corruption arrives when the denial of created kinds is applied to man. Genesis 1:27 names two, male and female, in the same chapter and the same grammar that names the kinds of tree and beast. A generation taught that biological categories are labels laid over a continuum has been handed, in advance, the premise that the categories of sex are labels too — assignable, revisable, self-declared. The two claims are one claim. Scripture’s answer is the same in both cases and is stated as fact rather than opinion: male and female created he them. The boundary is creational, embodied, and not ours to move. Where a person suffers real distress against that boundary, the church owes compassion, patient care, and the gospel — and owes it precisely because the sufferer is an image-bearer of the God who fixed the kinds.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

One Hebrew noun carries the weight in Genesis, and a Greek noun of family and stock carries it in the New Testament. Both name a lineage that breeds true, which is why the same vocabulary serves creation, clean-and-unclean law, and the resurrection argument.

expand to see more

Hebrew mīn (H4327) — kind, species, category; the boundary term of Genesis 1 and of the clean-and-unclean lists in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14.

Greek genos (G1085) — kind, race, family, stock, offspring; the root of English genus and generation.

The Hebrew phrase is l'mīnēhū, after his kind — a prepositional clause, not a bare noun, so the text speaks of reproduction according to a category rather than merely of a category.

Whose seed is in itself (Genesis 1:11) is the mechanism attached to the boundary: the kind is preserved because the seed is internal to it.

Usage

"Ten times in Genesis 1 creation proceeds after his kind — the most repeated phrase in the chapter, and therefore the most deliberate."

"Whose seed is in itself (Genesis 1:11) ties the boundary to the means of its own preservation."

"Paul argues the resurrection from the same premise: All flesh is not the same flesh (1 Corinthians 15:39). God assigns kinds, and He raises according to them."
